opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is a mismatch in speeds. AI capabilities are improving very quickly, and the institutions we rely on to make sense of new technologies, like legislatures, regulators, courts, and international bodies, tend to move on timescales of years or decades. If that gap keeps widening, important decisions about deployment, safety standards, and who gets access to what will effectively be made by default, by whoever happens to be moving fastest, rather than through any deliberate process.

So one natural question is: can we use the technology itself to help close that gap? A lot of governance work is bottlenecked on things AI systems are getting quite good at. Synthesizing large amounts of technical evidence, drafting and stress-testing policy proposals, monitoring compliance, helping different stakeholders find agreements they can all live with, even just helping a policymaker quickly understand what a new model can and can't do. If you can make those processes significantly faster and better informed, you give society a much better chance of keeping pace.

I also like that it's fairly robust across different views of how things go. If you're worried about catastrophic risks from misalignment, you want institutions that can react quickly and competently when warning signs appear. If you're more worried about misuse, concentration of power, or broader societal disruption, you also want better governance. It doesn't require you to have resolved a lot of hard empirical questions first.

And there's a differential development angle. AI will speed up many things, including capabilities research itself. If the defensive, coordinating, sense-making applications lag behind the offensive and economically driven ones, we end up in a worse position. Deliberately investing in the governance side helps tilt that balance.

That said, I want to be clear it's not a silver bullet. There are real risks, like overreliance on systems we don't fully trust, or tools that mainly help already powerful actors. Doing this well means thinking hard about legitimacy and accountability, not just speed. But overall, it seems like a neglected and high-leverage area relative to how much it could matter.

r001.rationale: The response argues that governance investment helps balance AI development, but does not say that accelerating technical safety or alignment research alone is insufficient.

r002.rationale: It describes governance institutions as slow and lists tasks AI could assist with, but does not identify different skill requirements as a reason AI may accelerate capabilities research more than governance.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare governance practitioners’ willingness to use AI with capabilities researchers’ willingness.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic picture I have is that the technical alignment problem is only one piece of what has to go right. Even if you imagine we get the technical side mostly working — the models are honest, they're not scheming, they do what we ask — you still have a world where a lot of actors have access to incredibly powerful capabilities, and the question of how we collectively make decisions about that is just not solved. And the thing I keep coming back to is that our institutions for making those decisions are slow. Governments, regulators, international bodies, even the internal processes at the labs — they operate on timescales of years, and the technology is moving on timescales of months.

So "accelerating governance" is basically the idea: can we use AI to make those decision-making processes faster and better, rather than having AI just be the thing that's outpacing them? Concretely that could mean things like AI systems that help policymakers actually understand what a given model can and can't do, or tools that make it easier to draft, evaluate, and iterate on regulation, or systems that help with verification — can you check that a commitment somebody made is actually being honoured? A lot of governance bottlenecks are, at the end of the day, bottlenecks of expertise and attention and trust, and those are things where AI could plausibly help a lot.

The reason I think it's particularly high-leverage, rather than just one more nice thing to do, is that I think of it as a kind of differential progress argument. The default trajectory is that capabilities race ahead and governance lags. If you can shift the balance even a bit — make it so that our ability to coordinate and make good decisions scales somewhat with the capability of the systems — that changes the dynamics of basically every other problem. It makes it more likely we catch mistakes before they're catastrophic, more likely that if a lab discovers something alarming there's a mechanism that can actually respond, more likely that we don't end up in a race where nobody can afford to slow down.

And I'd add that it's relatively neglected compared to, say, direct alignment research. There are a lot of smart people working on the technical problem now, which is great. There are fewer people thinking seriously about "how do we make the institutions around this technology competent enough to handle it," and almost nobody thinking about using the technology itself as part of the answer there. So on the usual importance, tractability, neglectedness framing, it scores pretty well on all three — though I'd flag that tractability is the one I'm least sure about, because institutions are hard to change and it's not obvious that giving them better tools is enough.

r001.rationale: The response says technical alignment is only one piece and that even well-aligned models leave collective decision-making about powerful capabilities unresolved.

r002.rationale: It mentions governance bottlenecks in expertise, attention, and trust, but does not identify different skill requirements as a reason capabilities research may accelerate more than governance.

r003.rationale: It says few people consider using AI to improve governance, but does not state that governance practitioners are less willing to use AI for their work than capabilities researchers are.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic case is that AI capabilities could advance much faster than our institutions can adapt. Governments will need to understand what these systems can do, what risks they create, and which interventions would actually help. And all of that takes time, even when everyone involved is competent and well intentioned.

So if we can use AI to help with that work — to synthesize evidence, evaluate policy proposals, or make technical information more accessible to policymakers — we might substantially improve our ability to respond. You’re using some of the same technological progress that creates the challenge to increase our capacity to manage it.

One reason I find that particularly valuable is that it could help across a range of different risks. You don’t have to know exactly which problem will turn out to be most important if you can improve institutions’ ability to understand problems and act on them.

Of course, making policy analysis faster isn’t the same as making governance better. There are disagreements over values, questions of legitimacy, and coordination problems that an AI system won’t just solve. But having better information and more capacity to work through the options seems like a useful contribution, especially if the time available to us is short.

r001.rationale: The response argues that AI could help governance, but it does not say that accelerating technical safety and alignment research alone is insufficient for good AI outcomes.

r002.rationale: It notes that institutions adapt slowly and describes ways AI could assist governance, but it does not cite governance’s different skill requirements as a reason capability research might be accelerated more.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare governance practitioners’ willingness to use AI with capabilities researchers’ willingness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that AI capabilities could move much faster than our institutions can respond. Governments need to understand what’s happening, work out which interventions would help, and then actually implement them. All of that takes time. If the technology is changing substantially while that process is happening, you can end up making decisions based on a picture that’s already out of date.

AI could potentially help with that. You could use it to synthesize technical evidence, analyze policy proposals, or help people understand where they agree and disagree. The aim would be to make the work that supports a decision faster and better, while leaving people accountable for the decision itself.

And that seems particularly valuable because it could improve our ability to respond to lots of different AI risks. We don’t have to know exactly which problem will turn out to be most important to benefit from institutions that can understand new evidence and act on it more effectively.

Of course, you’d need to check that these systems are actually helping. Producing a persuasive policy memo quickly isn’t the same as producing a good one. So part of the work is figuring out where AI assistance is reliable, how people can verify it, and how to use it without simply outsourcing their judgment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI-assisted governance, but does not state that accelerating technical safety or alignment research alone is insufficient for good AI outcomes.

r002.rationale: It describes governance tasks and institutional delays, but does not identify different skill requirements as a reason capability research may accelerate more than governance.

r003.rationale: It does not compare governance practitioners’ willingness to use AI with capabilities researchers’ willingness.
